sections.text: ## Frederick Douglass (1818–1895)

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: ### Who He Was

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: Douglass was born into slavery in Maryland, taught himself to read (against the law), escaped in 1838 at age 20, and became the most effective antislavery voice in America. His *Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave* (1845) was a bestseller. He founded the *North Star* newspaper in 1847. He advised Lincoln during the Civil War. He later served as US Marshal for the District of Columbia, Minister to Haiti.

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: ### What He Did

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: **Testimony as political weapon**: The basic problem of abolitionism was that most Northern white Americans had never met a slave and could abstract away the human reality. Douglass's speeches and *Narrative* made that abstraction impossible. He was articulate, educated, and could describe the physical reality of slavery with precision.

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: **The 1852 speech ("What to the Slave is the Fourth of July?")**:

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
```
  "This Fourth [of] July is *yours*, not *mine*. You may rejoice,
   I must mourn... What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July?
   I answer: a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in
   the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the
   constant victim."

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
RHETORICAL STRATEGY:
  - Begins by praising the Founders sincerely
  - Establishes his own patriotism ("I do not despair of this country")
  - Then: the hypocrisy is not hidden; it is the explicit argument
  - Turns the Declaration's language into an indictment
  - Same move Jefferson planted: universal language ↔ slavery = permanent contradiction
```

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: **The argument on slavery's illegality**: Douglass, unlike Garrison, argued that the Constitution *could* be read as an antislavery document — that the Fifth Amendment's "due process" clause protected enslaved people's liberty as much as anyone else's. This was the NAACP's eventual legal strategy: not that the Constitution was pro-slavery and should be replaced, but that it contained the tools for its own antislavery interpretation.

sections.text: ### What He Did

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: Du Bois was the first African American to receive a PhD from Harvard (1895). He spent 70 years as a public intellectual, sociologist, civil rights activist, and propagandist.

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: **Key contributions:**

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
| Work | Year | What It Did |
|------|------|-------------|
| *The Philadelphia Negro* | 1899 | First rigorous sociological study of a Black community in America; established empirical study of race |
| *The Souls of Black Folk* | 1903 | Introduced "double consciousness"; defined the internal experience of Black Americans |
| NAACP founding | 1909 | With white progressives (Jane Addams, Oswald Villard); institutional vehicle for legal challenges |
| *The Crisis* (journal) | 1910–1934 | NAACP's journal; 100,000 circulation by 1920; public opinion formation |
| *Black Reconstruction in America* | 1935 | Demolished the "Dunning School" historiography that portrayed Reconstruction as a failure due to Black incompetence |
| *The Souls of Black Folk* (double consciousness) | 1903 | Intellectual framework still in use |

```
sections.text: ## Rosa Parks (1913–2005)

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: ### What She Did — and What Is Misunderstood

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: Rosa Parks did not sit down because she was tired. She was the secretary of the Montgomery NAACP chapter and had been trained at the Highlander Folk School in Tennessee (a civil rights training center). Her arrest on December 1, 1955, was not spontaneous — she was selected as a test case because she was a respectable, dignified figure who would make an effective plaintiff.

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
```
  THE MONTGOMERY BUS BOYCOTT AS ORGANIZATIONAL CASE STUDY
  =========================================================

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
THE PREPARATION:
  - E.D. Nixon (NAACP leader): had been looking for the right test case
  - Claudette Colvin (15, pregnant, arrested March 1955): rejected
    as test case because of complications in her situation
  - Parks: secretary of NAACP; known figure; excellent plaintiff

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
THE ORGANIZATION:
  - Women's Political Council (Jo Ann Robinson): printed and
    distributed 52,000 leaflets in one night
  - Nixon + Abernathy: called first mass meeting
  - MLK: chosen to lead MIA (Montgomery Improvement Assoc.)
    — partly because he was new, had no enemies yet

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
THE ECONOMICS:
  - Black riders = 75% of Montgomery bus ridership
  - 382-day boycott: economically devastating to bus company
  - Alternative transportation: carpool network organized through
    Black churches; insurance policy written in Lloyd's of London
    (white insurers refused)

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
THE LEGAL:
  - Browder v. Gayle filed separately: 4 women plaintiffs
  - Won at district court; upheld by Supreme Court (1956)
  - Browder v. Gayle desegregated Montgomery buses
  - Rosa Parks's arrest was the organizing catalyst; the legal
    case used different plaintiffs
```

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: Parks spent the rest of her life working in Rep. John Conyers's office in Detroit. She is one of the most misrepresented figures in American civil rights history — her active role as organizer is erased in favor of the myth of the tired seamstress.

sections.text: ## Martin Luther King Jr. (1929–1968)

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: ### What He Did

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: King's specific contributions: (1) synthesized the Gandhian nonviolent resistance framework with the Black church tradition; (2) generated media images that made the violence of white supremacy visible to a national (and international) audience; (3) maintained the coalition between Black activists, white liberals, and labor unions that was necessary for legislative success.

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: **The Birmingham Campaign (1963)**: The strategic decision that turned the movement:

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
```
  BIRMINGHAM CAMPAIGN: STRATEGIC DESIGN
  ========================================

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
Problem: Birmingham was the most segregated city in America.
           Bull Connor (Public Safety Commissioner): known
           for using violence.

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
Strategy (James Lawson + SCLC):
  Provoke violent response → make it visible → political crisis

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
Execution:
  - Marches in defiance of court injunctions
  - April 12, 1963: King arrested (writes "Letter from
    Birmingham Jail")
  - "Project C" (Confrontation): school children march
    May 2-3: Connor uses fire hoses and police dogs
    on children as young as 6
  - Photos published worldwide; international condemnation
  - Kennedy administration forced to act

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
Result:
  - Kennedy proposes Civil Rights Act (June 11, 1963)
  - Birmingham merchants negotiate settlement
  - August 28: March on Washington; "I Have a Dream"

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
THE MECHANISM: Nonviolence as media strategy
  Connor's violence, made visible = political pressure on JFK
  JFK's political pressure = Civil Rights Act (July 2, 1964)
```

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: **"Letter from Birmingham Jail" (April 16, 1963)**: Written in the margins of a newspaper and smuggled out. Addressed to white moderate clergymen who had criticized the demonstrations as "unwise and untimely."

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
```
  KEY ARGUMENT:
  "One who breaks an unjust law must do so openly, lovingly,
   and with a willingness to accept the penalty."

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
Distinction between just and unjust law:
  "A just law is a man-made code that squares with the moral
   law or the law of God. An unjust law is a code that is
   out of harmony with the moral law."

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
On the "white moderate":
  "I have almost reached the regrettable conclusion that the
   Negro's great stumbling block in his stride toward freedom
   is not the White Citizen's Council or the Ku Klux Klanner,
   but the white moderate, who prefers a negative peace which
   is the absence of tension to a positive peace which is the
   presence of justice."
```

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: ### King's Evolution (1965–68)

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: After the Voting Rights Act (1965), King moved to address economic inequality directly — and lost much of his coalition:

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
- **Chicago Open Housing Campaign (1966)**: Attempted to extend civil rights movement to Northern residential segregation. Met by angry white mobs in Marquette Park; failed to achieve lasting change.
- **Riverside Church speech (April 4, 1967)**: Opposed the Vietnam War publicly — alienated President Johnson, lost support of *New York Times* editorial board, cost movement significant funding.
- **Poor People's Campaign (1968)**: Multi-racial coalition of poor Americans; march on Washington. King was killed April 4, 1968, in Memphis while supporting striking sanitation workers.

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: The sanitized "I Have a Dream" MLK obscures the late-career MLK who was calling capitalism into question and organizing a cross-racial poor people's coalition.

sections.text: ### What He Did

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: Malcolm X (born Malcolm Little; took the name El-Hajj Malik el-Shabazz) provided the alternative frame to King's integrationist nonviolence. His contribution is strategic and intellectual, not legislative.

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: **The Nation of Islam phase (1952–64)**: Built the NOI from ~400 to 30,000 members as its most effective organizer and speaker. Core message: integration is not the goal; Black self-determination and separation is.

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
```
  MALCOLM X'S STRATEGIC CRITIQUE OF KING
  =========================================

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
Malcolm:                          King:
  "Black nationalism"               Integration into American society
  Self-defense ("by any means       Nonviolence as strategic principle
   necessary")
  Economic self-sufficiency         Coalition with white liberals
   within Black community
  Critique of white liberalism      Appeal to white liberal conscience
  (Northern liberals as             as necessary coalition partner
   hypocrites)

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
BOTH were partially right:
  - Malcolm was right that Northern segregation was not
    being addressed by Southern civil rights strategy
  - Malcolm was right that white liberal support was
    unreliable and often self-serving
  - King was right that nonviolence + coalition was the
    politically achievable path to legislation
  - King was right that the ballot was the primary tool
    available
```

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: **The evolution (1964–65)**: After breaking with Elijah Muhammad and completing the Hajj to Mecca, Malcolm moved toward a more universal human rights framework. His organization of Afro-American Unity: "The struggle of the African-American is not simply a struggle for civil rights but a human rights issue." He was assassinated February 21, 1965, by NOI gunmen, before he could develop this evolution.

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: **Malcolm's structural contribution**: He made King's position look *moderate* to white America, which helped King. He also articulated the limits of integrationist strategy and the reality of Northern structural racism in ways that Congress and the Kennedy/Johnson administrations could not ignore.

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: ## Nelson Mandela (1918–2013)

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: ### What He Did — Two Phases

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: **Phase 1: ANC Militant (1944–1964)**: Mandela co-founded the ANC Youth League in 1944, organized the Defiance Campaign (1952), and after the Sharpeville Massacre (1960) concluded that nonviolent resistance was insufficient against a regime willing to shoot peaceable protesters. He co-founded Umkhonto we Sizwe (Spear of the Nation — the ANC's armed wing) and organized sabotage campaigns (not attacks on people). Arrested 1962; sentenced to life imprisonment at Rivonia Trial (1964).

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: **Phase 2: Prisoner (1964–1990)**: 27 years on Robben Island and later Pollsmoor Prison. The ANC kept his name and image alive internationally. The "Free Mandela" campaign became the focal point of anti-apartheid organizing globally. His refusal of conditional release offers (unless the ANC renounced violence) maintained his moral authority.

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela
Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
THE ACTORS:
  F.W. de Klerk (Nationalist President): realized apartheid was
  economically and diplomatically untenable
  Mandela: recognized that negotiations required credible
           commitment from both sides

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
THE RISKS:
  - Right-wing Afrikaner white extremists (AWB) threatened
    civil war
  - ANC military wing wanted more radical transfer
  - Inkatha Freedom Party (Buthelezi) violence in KwaZulu-Natal
  - Communist Party in ANC coalition had different agenda
  - International investors requiring stability

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
THE MECHANISMS:
  - Mandela called for national reconciliation, not revenge
    → This was strategic: revenge = spiral; reconciliation = stability
  - Truth and Reconciliation Commission (post-1994):
    Amnesty for full disclosure vs. prosecution; not amnesty vs. nothing
  - Government of National Unity: ANC + NP + IFP in cabinet
    → Managed transition; prevented capital flight
  - Stepped down after one term (1999)
    → Established the norm; enormous symbolic weight

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
KEY DECISION: Mandela refused to become a permanent leader.
  One term. Thabo Mbeki succeeded through ANC democratic process.
  Contrast: Mugabe (Zimbabwe) — liberation hero becomes autocrat.
```

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: ### Truth and Reconciliation Commission

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: The TRC (chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu) granted amnesty to perpetrators who made full public disclosure of politically motivated crimes. The trade was:

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
- Full public confession → amnesty
- Silence or partial disclosure → possible prosecution

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: This was not amnesia. It was *structured* public accounting. Victims' families heard what happened. Perpetrators had to confess publicly. The political calculation: South Africa needed the security forces to stand down, not fight a last-ditch war. Prosecution would drive them to desperate resistance. Public confession with amnesty was the least-bad option.

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text: Critics (including many victims) argued it gave too much to perpetrators. Defenders argued it maintained the transition to democracy without a race war.

sections.text: ## Comparison Table

metadata.title: Civil Rights: Douglass, Du Bois, MLK, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Mandela

sections.text:
| Figure | Era | Primary Method | Legislative/Institutional Result |
|--------|-----|---------------|----------------------------------|
| Douglass | 1845–1895 | Testimony, journalism, oratory | 13th Amendment (coalition work with Lincoln) |
| Du Bois | 1903–1963 | Scholarship + journalism + NAACP | NAACP legal strategy framework |
| Rosa Parks | 1955 | Strategic test case | Browder v. Gayle (bus desegregation) |
| MLK | 1955–1968 | Nonviolent provocation of media-visible violence | Civil Rights Act (1964), Voting Rights Act (1965) |
| Malcolm X | 1952–1965 | Radical alternative frame; Black nationalism | Moved Overton window; articulated Northern racism |
| Mandela | 1944–1999 | Armed resistance → negotiated transition | End of apartheid; TRC; democratic South Africa |
